newsitem.title: USA: Incinerator subsidy bill advances in Ill. House.
newsitem.headline: Incinerator subsidy bill advances in Ill. House.

text.p: An Illinois House committee Tuesday advanced a bill that would restore a state subsidy to two bond-financed waste-to-energy incinerators.
Following a hearing on the measure, House Public Utilities Committee voted 6-5 to move the bill onto the House floor.
The bill faces opposition from House Speaker Michael Madigan, D-Chicago.
A representative from an environmental group who testified at the hearing said he doubted the bill would ultimately pass.

"I think it's not going to become law," said Alexander Ewing, staff attorney for the Chicago-based Environmental Law & Policy Center. "At a time (the state is) trying desparately to scrap together some nickles to fund schools, to give $700 million to incinerators to pollute the air is so appalling to conceive that it would become law."
Ewing said he and a representative of Foster Wheeler Corp, the developer of an incinerator in the Chicago suburb of Robbins, were the only ones to testify before the House committee.
A spokesman for Clinton, N.J.-based Foster Wheeler was not available for comment.

Incinerators in Robbins and in Ford Heights, another Chicago suburb, would be the only facilities to benefit under the bill that would restore a state subsidy that was repealed by the General Assembly last year.

That subsidy guaranteed incinerators a higher rate at which they could sell the electricity they produced to utilities. The Environmental Law & Policy Center has estimated returning the subsidy to the two incinerators would cost the state more than $700 million over a 20-year period.

The subsidy's repeal imperiled nearly $500 million of tax-exempt, unrated bonds that were sold for three projects. However, only the Robbins and Ford Heights facilities were financed, built and had received necessary government orders and permits -- a stipulation of the bill to restore the subsidy.
The bill now has until April 25 to make it out of the House and into the Senate, according to a legislative information office.
A top aide to Gov. Jim Edgar, who signed the subsidy repeal into law a year ago, has said it was "highly unlikely" the governor would change his mind about the subsidy.
Meanmwhile, developers of four incinerators have lawsuits pending in state courts challenging the subsidy's repeal.
